lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Stainless steel is everywhere in Africa: food processing plants in Kenya, dairy equipment in South Africa, chemical tanks in Nigeria, and architectural railings in Egypt. Unlike mild steel, stainless steel contains at least 10.5% chromium, which forms a protective oxide layer that resists rust. But that same chromium makes welding tricky. If you weld it wrong, you get 'sensitization' â chromium carbide precipitates at grain boundaries, leaving the steel vulnerable to corrosion. In Africa's humid coastal cities like Mombasa or Lagos, a bad stainless weld can rust through in months.

You need to care because stainless steel jobs pay better. A skilled stainless welder in Nairobi can earn 2-3 times more than a mild steel welder. Industries like breweries (e.g., East African Breweries), dairies (Brookside), and hospitals need sanitary stainless piping and tanks. The demand is high, but the supply of trained welders is low. This module will teach you the specific techniques â TIG welding with DCEN, back purging, controlled heat input â that make stainless welds last.

We'll focus on 304 and 316 stainless, the most common grades in Africa. 304 is for general use; 316 has molybdenum for chloride resistance, essential for coastal or chemical environments. You'll learn to set your machine, choose filler rods (308L for 304, 316L for 316), and avoid the mistakes that cause cracking and corrosion. By the end, you'll be able to weld a stainless steel water tank that passes a pressure test and a visual inspection.

This isn't theory. Every lesson is practical, using tools you can find in any African welding shop: an inverter TIG machine, argon gas, ceriated tungsten, and stainless filler rods. You'll practice on scrap before working on real jobs. Remember: stainless steel is expensive, so measure twice, weld once. Let's get started.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To weld stainless steel properly, you need a TIG (Tungsten Inert Gas) welder with DCEN (Direct Current Electrode Negative). A 200-amp inverter TIG machine is ideal; brands like Miller, Lincoln, or local Chinese imports (e.g., Riland) work. You'll also need a foot pedal or torch switch to control amperage. For stainless, amperage ranges from 40-80 amps for 1.6mm sheet, up to 120-150 amps for 6mm plate. Always use pure argon gas (99.99% purity) at 8-12 litres per minute flow rate. In Africa, gas suppliers like BOC or Afrox can refill your cylinder.

Tungsten electrodes: use 2% ceriated (grey tip) or 1.5% lanthanated (gold tip). They handle DC better than pure tungsten. Grind the tungsten to a sharp point, lengthwise, on a dedicated grinding wheel (never use the same wheel for steel, to avoid contamination). For filler rods, match the base metal: ER308L for 304 stainless, ER316L for 316. Rod diameters: 1.6mm for thin sheet, 2.4mm for thicker sections. You'll also need a stainless steel wire brush (never use a carbon steel brush) and acetone or denatured alcohol for cleaning.

Other essentials: a gas lens kit for better argon coverage, a #7 or #8 ceramic cup, and a back purge setup if welding pipes or tanks. Back purging uses argon inside the pipe to prevent oxidation on the backside of the weld. You can make a simple purge dam with aluminum foil and tape. For cutting stainless, use a plasma cutter or an angle grinder with a stainless-specific cutting disc (not the same disc you use for mild steel).

Personal protective equipment: auto-darkening welding helmet (shade 9-11 for TIG), leather gloves, and a respirator. Stainless welding produces hexavalent chromium fumes, which are carcinogenic. In a closed shop in Johannesburg or Cairo, you must have fume extraction or good ventilation. Finally, a stainless steel scratch brush and pickling paste (or a citric acid gel) for post-weld cleaning. These tools are available from welding supply shops in most African cities; if not, order online from suppliers like Weldability or Amazon.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Clean the metal. Stainless must be spotless. Wipe the joint and 25mm around it with acetone. Remove any oil, grease, or marker ink. Use a new stainless wire brush to scrub the surface. Do not use a brush that has touched carbon steel â it will embed iron particles and cause rust.

Step 2: Set up your machine. For 2mm stainless sheet, set the TIG machine to DCEN, 60-80 amps. Set argon flow to 10 L/min. Grind your ceriated tungsten to a sharp point. Install a #7 gas lens cup. If welding pipe or a tank, set up back purging: seal one end, flow argon at 5 L/min into the other end for 2 minutes before welding. Use a oxygen meter to check that oxygen is below 1% inside.

Step 3: Tack weld. Clamp the pieces together. Use the same settings. Make small tacks every 50mm. For thin sheet, use a heat sink (aluminum block) behind the joint to prevent warping. Let each tack cool before the next. Check alignment with a square.

Step 4: Weld the joint. For butt welds on 2mm sheet, use a keyhole technique: start at one end, create a small keyhole (a hole that opens up), then move forward, adding filler rod as you go. Dip the rod into the leading edge of the puddle. Keep the torch angle at 70-80 degrees, pushing forward. For lap joints, direct the arc at the edge of the top plate to melt both. For T-joints, angle the torch 45 degrees and add filler to the corner. Maintain a tight arc (tungsten 2-3mm from the work). Move steadily; if you go too slow, you'll burn through; too fast, you'll get incomplete fusion.

Step 5: Post-weld cleaning. After welding, the weld and heat-affected zone will have a rainbow tint (oxidation). Brush with a stainless wire brush. For critical applications, apply pickling paste (contains nitric and hydrofluoric acid â wear gloves and goggles) or use an electrochemical cleaning machine. Rinse with water after 10-20 minutes. For sanitary welds, you may need to grind and polish the weld to a smooth finish.

Step 6: Inspect. Look for undercut, porosity, or cracks. A good stainless weld is shiny and has a smooth, consistent bead. If you see black spots, you had too much heat or poor gas coverage. Practice on scrap until you can produce a consistent bead.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Using the wrong gas. Some welders try to use CO2 or a CO2/argon mix (like MIG gas) for TIG. That will cause carbon pickup and corrosion. Fix: Always use pure argon (99.99%). If you only have a MIG machine, you can use it with stainless wire and a tri-mix gas (90% helium, 7.5% argon, 2.5% CO2), but TIG is preferred.

Mistake 2: Too much heat. Stainless has low thermal conductivity, so heat stays in the weld zone. If you use the same amperage as mild steel, you'll burn through or cause distortion. Fix: Reduce amperage by 20-30% compared to mild steel. Use a foot pedal to ramp down at the end. For thin sheet, use a heat sink or pulse mode.

Mistake 3: No back purge. When welding pipes or tanks, the backside of the weld oxidizes (sugaring) if not protected. That sugar is a corrosion site. Fix: Always back purge with argon. If you can't purge, use a flux-coated rod (like E308L-16) for stick welding, but that's only for non-critical work.

Mistake 4: Contaminated tungsten. If you dip the tungsten into the puddle, it gets contaminated and the arc wanders. Fix: Stop, remove the tungsten, break off the contaminated tip, regrind, and restart. Keep a dedicated grinder for tungsten.

Mistake 5: Using carbon steel brushes. That embeds iron into the stainless surface, causing rust spots. Fix: Use only stainless steel brushes, and keep them separate.

Mistake 6: Welding without cleaning. Oil, paint, or marker ink causes porosity and cracks. Fix: Clean with acetone and a stainless brush before welding.

Mistake 7: Fast cooling. Quenching a hot stainless weld with water can cause cracking. Fix: Let it air cool, or use a heat sink to draw heat away slowly.

Mistake 8: Wrong filler rod. Using mild steel filler on stainless will rust and crack. Fix: Match the filler to the base metal: 308L for 304, 316L for 316.

If you make a mistake, don't panic. Grind out the bad weld and start again. Stainless is forgiving if you follow the rules.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Welding stainless steel produces hexavalent chromium and nickel fumes, which can cause cancer, asthma, and skin irritation. In Africa, many workshops are poorly ventilated. You must protect yourself. Always weld in a well-ventilated area or use a fume extractor. A simple fan blowing fumes away from your breathing zone helps, but it can disrupt shielding gas. Better: use a respirator with P100 filters. 3M or Honeywell respirators are available in most African cities. If you smell a sweet, metallic taste, you're breathing fumes â stop and ventilate.

Arc rays from TIG welding are intense. Use an auto-darkening helmet with a shade 9-11 for stainless. Never look at the arc without a helmet. Wear leather gloves, a leather apron, and closed shoes. TIG welding produces less spatter than stick, but the arc can still burn you. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. In a shop with wood or fabric, clear the area of flammable materials.

Gas safety: Argon is an asphyxiant. It's heavier than air, so it can pool in low areas (pits, tanks). If you're welding inside a tank, you must have forced ventilation and a safety watch outside. Never use argon to 'cool' yourself â it can cause immediate suffocation. Check cylinders for leaks with soapy water. Secure cylinders upright with a chain.

Electrical safety: TIG machines use high frequency for arc starting. Keep your gloves dry. Ground the work piece properly. Don't weld in wet conditions. In countries with unstable power (e.g., Nigeria), use a voltage stabilizer to protect your machine.

Best practices: Plan your welds to minimize distortion. Use the least amount of heat possible. Clean as you go. Label your stainless brushes and tools so they don't get contaminated. After welding, clean the weld with a stainless brush and pickling paste. For food-grade work, passivate the surface with citric acid. Document your settings for each job â amperage, gas flow, filler rod â so you can repeat good results. Finally, practice on scrap before welding a customer's expensive stainless part. A small mistake can cost thousands of naira or shillings.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Exercise: Weld a 304 stainless steel water tank. You will need two pieces of 2mm thick 304 stainless sheet, each 300mm x 300mm. You will form a 90-degree corner and weld the seam. This simulates a real tank corner. Tools: TIG welder (200A), pure argon cylinder, 2% ceriated tungsten (2.4mm), #7 gas lens cup, ER308L filler rod (1.6mm), stainless wire brush, acetone, clamps, and a heat sink (aluminum block).

Step 1: Clean both sheets with acetone and a stainless brush. Mark a 10mm bend line on each sheet. Using a sheet metal brake or a hammer and angle iron, bend a 90-degree flange on each sheet. The flanges should be 10mm wide. Clamp the two flanges together to form a corner. Check for a tight fit â gaps should be less than 0.5mm.

Step 2: Set up your TIG machine. DCEN, 70 amps. Argon flow 10 L/min. Grind tungsten to a sharp point. If you have a foot pedal, set it to control amperage. Place an aluminum heat sink behind the joint to prevent warping. Tack weld at both ends and in the middle. Let each tack cool.

Step 3: Weld the seam. Start at one end. Use a keyhole technique: create a small keyhole at the start, then move forward, adding filler rod with a dip-and-move rhythm. Keep the arc tight. The weld should be a smooth, concave bead. If you burn through, stop, let it cool, and reduce amperage to 60. If you get a convex bead, you're adding too much filler; use less.

Step 4: After welding, inspect the weld. It should have a light gold or straw color, not black or grey. If black, you had too much heat or poor gas coverage. Brush the weld with a stainless brush. Apply pickling paste if available, or use a citric acid gel. Let it sit for 15 minutes, then rinse.

Step 5: Test for leaks. Fill the tank with water and check for leaks. If you find a leak, mark it, grind it out, and re-weld. For a food-grade tank, you may need to polish the weld. Repeat this exercise with 316 stainless and ER316L filler. Practice until you can produce a consistent, leak-free weld. This skill is in high demand for dairy and brewery tanks across Africa.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Welding Stainless Steel in African Fabrication Workshops

This practical reference supports the Advanced Welding Techniques module on Welding Stainless Steel. It is written for working welders, workshop owners, and technical trainers who need to win and deliver stainless steel contracts in African markets â from dairy and food processing plants in Kenya, to breweries in Nigeria, to water treatment and mining fabrication in South Africa and Zambia. Stainless steel work pays a premium because it demands control: heat control, cleanliness, consumable selection, and post-weld treatment. Get these right and your workshop can quote confidently for hygienic, corrosion-resistant fabrication. Get them wrong and you deliver cracking, discolouration, and rust â the fastest way to lose a client.

This lesson is a condensed field manual. Use it at the bench, not just in the classroom. It covers the practical parameters, a comparison of processes, data tables with real sources, a safety warning, a checklist, and links to free official references.

Process Selection: Matching the Method to the Job

In African fabrication shops, three processes dominate stainless steel work: TIG (GTAW), MIG (GMAW), and manual metal arc (MMA/SMAW). TIG gives the cleanest, most controllable weld and is preferred for thin sheet, hygienic pipework, and visible architectural work. MIG is faster for thicker sections and longer runs. MMA is portable and useful on site where gas supply is unreliable, but produces more spatter and slag. The table below compares them for stainless steel.

Table 1: Process selection for stainless steel (typical workshop parameters)
Process Typical thickness Current / polarity Shielding gas Best for Limitations
TIG (GTAW) 0.5â6 mm DCEN (DCâ) Argon 100% (or Ar + 2% Hâ) Thin sheet, pipe root, food-grade, visible joints Slow, needs skill, gas-dependent
MIG (GMAW) 3â12 mm DCEP (DC+) Ar + 2% Oâ or Ar + 2% COâ (tri-mix for some) Thicker plate, production runs, structural More spatter, less root control
MMA / SMAW 3â12 mm DCEP (DC+) Flux coating (no external gas) Site work, repair, no-gas environments Slag, higher heat input, more cleanup

Sources: TWI Ltd, "What is the difference between TIG and MIG welding?"; Lincoln Electric, "Stainless Steel Welding"; ESAB Africa, "How to Weld Stainless Steel".

Practical Parameters and Consumables

The single biggest cause of failed stainless welds in small workshops is heat input. Stainless steel conducts heat slowly and expands more than carbon steel. Too much heat causes distortion, carbide precipitation (sensitisation), and loss of corrosion resistance. Too little causes lack of fusion. The table below gives starting parameters you can tune to your machine and material.

Table 2: Starting parameters for TIG welding austenitic stainless steel (304 / 316L)
Thickness Amperage (A) Tungsten (2% thoriated / lanthanated) Filler rod Gas flow (Argon) Joint prep
1.0 mm30â501.6 mm1.6 mm ER308L8â10 L/minSquare butt, no gap
1.5 mm50â801.6 mm1.6 mm ER308L8â10 L/minSquare butt, 0â1 mm gap
3.0 mm90â1302.4 mm2.4 mm ER308L10â12 L/minV-groove 60Â°, 1.5 mm root face
6.0 mm140â2002.4 mm2.4 mm ER308L12â15 L/minV-groove 60Â°, 2 mm root face
Pipe root (any)70â1102.4 mm2.4 mm ER308L10â12 L/min + purgeOpen root, 2â3 mm gap

Sources: Lincoln Electric, ER308L/ER316L consumable data sheets; TWI Ltd, "Heat Input and Welding"; ESAB Africa, "How to Weld Stainless Steel". Always confirm against your machine's manual and the material certificate.

Key Practical Rules for the Bench

  • Cleanliness is everything. Stainless steel must be free of oil, grease, paint, and carbon steel contamination. Use dedicated stainless-only wire brushes, grinding discs, and gloves. A carbon steel brush will embed iron and cause rust.
  • Control heat input. Use the lowest amperage that gives full fusion. Interpass temperature should stay below 150 Â°C. For 316L, this reduces sensitisation.
  • Purge the back of the weld. For pipe and hygienic work, back-purge with argon to prevent oxidation (sugaring) on the inside surface. This is non-negotiable for food and dairy clients.
  • Use the right filler. Match filler to base metal: ER308L for 304, ER316L for 316. Never use carbon steel filler on stainless.
  • Post-weld cleaning. Remove heat tint by pickling, passivation, or mechanical methods. Heat tint destroys the passive chromium oxide layer and is the starting point for corrosion.
  • Distortion control. Use tack welds, balanced sequences, and heat sinks. Stainless moves more than mild steel.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Hexavalent Chromium and Welding Fumes

Welding stainless steel produces fumes containing hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) and nickel, which are carcinogenic and can cause asthma and skin sensitisation. In enclosed African workshop conditions â common where ventilation is poor â this risk is high. Always: weld with local exhaust ventilation or fume extraction at the arc; wear a powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) or at minimum a P100/FFP3 respirator; keep your head out of the fume plume; and never weld in a confined space without forced ventilation and a spotter. Also protect against arc radiation (UV) with proper helmet shade (minimum shade 10â13 for TIG), and cover exposed skin. Source: US OSHA, "Hexavalent Chromium"; UK HSE, "Welding FAQs".

Business-First Notes for African Workshops

Stainless steel work is a margin opportunity. Food and beverage processors, dairies, breweries, pharmaceutical plants, and water utilities across Africa need hygienic stainless fabrication and repair. They pay for reliability and documentation. To win and keep this work:

  • Quote with a procedure. Present a simple welding procedure specification (WPS) and, where required, a welder qualification record. Clients in regulated sectors (food, pharma) increasingly ask for this.
  • Invest in gas supply. A reliable argon cylinder or bulk supply is the single biggest enabler of quality stainless work. Partner with a local gas supplier such as Afrox (South Africa) or regional distributors.
  • Train on scrap before production. Run test coupons, cut and etch them, and check penetration. This reduces rework and protects your reputation.
  • Price for post-weld treatment. Pickling paste, passivation chemicals, and labour are real costs. Include them.
  • Keep records. Material certificates, filler batch numbers, and gas purity records protect you if a client disputes corrosion failure.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Confirm base metal grade (304, 316L, etc.) and match filler (ER308L / ER316L).
  2. Clean joint and surrounding 25 mm with stainless-only tools; remove all oil, paint, and carbon steel contamination.
  3. Set amperage from Table 2 and verify on a test coupon before production.
  4. Set argon flow (8â15 L/min) and check for leaks; use a gas lens for better coverage.
  5. Back-purge pipe and hygienic joints with argon to prevent sugaring.
  6. Control interpass temperature (below 150 Â°C) and use balanced weld sequence to limit distortion.
  7. Inspect for heat tint, undercut, and lack of fusion; remove tint by pickling or mechanical cleaning.
  8. Passivate the weld and HAZ to restore corrosion resistance before handover.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • TWI Ltd â Tungsten Inert Gas Welding (TIG/GTAW)
  • Lincoln Electric â Stainless Steel Welding Guide
  • ESAB Africa â How to Weld Stainless Steel
  • US OSHA â Hexavalent Chromium Safety
  • UK HSE â Welding Safety FAQs

Prepared for the Rise AFRICA Skills course "Advanced Welding Techniques", module "Welding Stainless Steel". Always follow your local national standards (e.g. SANS 10162, EN 1090, AWS D1.6) and your machine manufacturer's instructions.

quiz.q: What is the minimum chromium content in stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel must contain at least 10.5% chromium to form a protective oxide layer.

quiz.q: Which gas is used for TIG welding stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: Pure argon is used for TIG welding stainless steel to prevent oxidation.

quiz.q: What is the correct polarity for TIG welding stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: DCEN (Direct Current Electrode Negative) provides deeper penetration and less heat on the tungsten.

quiz.q: Which filler rod is used for welding 304 stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: ER308L is matched to 304 stainless steel for corrosion resistance and strength.

quiz.q: What is back purging?
options: A) Cleaning the back of the weld
B) Using argon on the backside of the weld
quiz.explanation: Back purging uses argon to shield the backside of the weld from oxidation.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using a carbon steel brush on stainless?
options: B) It embeds iron particles causing rust
quiz.explanation: Carbon steel brushes leave iron particles that cause rust on stainless steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for TIG welding 2mm stainless sheet?
quiz.explanation: 60-80 amps is typical for 2mm stainless steel sheet.

quiz.q: What type of tungsten electrode is best for DC TIG welding stainless?
quiz.explanation: 2% ceriated tungsten provides good arc stability and longevity on DC.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of welding stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: Stainless welding produces hexavalent chromium fumes, which are carcinogenic.

quiz.q: What is sensitization in stainless steel?
options: B) Chromium carbide precipitation at grain boundaries
quiz.explanation: Sensitization occurs when chromium carbides form at grain boundaries, reducing corrosion resistance.

quiz.q: Which stainless steel grade is best for coastal environments?
quiz.explanation: 316 contains molybdenum, which improves resistance to chlorides in coastal areas.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a gas lens?
options: B) To provide better argon coverage
quiz.explanation: A gas lens creates a laminar flow of argon for better shielding coverage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you contaminate your tungsten?
options: B) Break off the tip and regrind
quiz.explanation: Contaminated tungsten causes an unstable arc; you must remove the contaminated part and regrind.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to clean stainless steel before welding?
options: B) Use acetone and a stainless brush
C) Use a carbon steel brush
quiz.explanation: Acetone removes oils and a stainless brush removes surface contaminants without embedding iron.

quiz.q: What is the recommended argon flow rate for TIG welding stainless?
quiz.explanation: 8-12 litres per minute provides adequate shielding without turbulence.

quiz.q: What is a keyhole technique used for?
options: B) Welding thin sheet without burn-through
quiz.explanation: The keyhole technique helps control heat and ensure full penetration on thin materials.

quiz.q: Why should you use a heat sink when welding stainless?
quiz.explanation: A heat sink absorbs heat to minimize distortion and warping.

quiz.q: What color should a good stainless TIG weld be?
quiz.explanation: A light gold or straw color indicates proper heat input and shielding.

quiz.q: What is pickling paste used for?
options: A) Cleaning and passivating stainless welds
C) Removing rust from carbon steel
quiz.explanation: Pickling paste removes oxidation and restores the passive layer on stainless steel.

quiz.q: Why is argon dangerous in a confined space?
quiz.explanation: Argon is an asphyxiant that can displace oxygen and cause suffocation.

quiz.q: What is the correct filler rod for 316 stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: ER316L matches the composition of 316 stainless steel for corrosion resistance.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of porosity in stainless welds?
quiz.explanation: Oil, grease, or dirt on the base metal causes porosity.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a TIG welding helmet?
quiz.explanation: Shade 9-11 is appropriate for TIG welding stainless steel.

quiz.q: What should you do if you burn through a thin stainless sheet?
options: B) Stop, let cool, reduce amperage, and re-weld
quiz.explanation: Reducing amperage and allowing cooling prevents further burn-through.

quiz.q: Why is stainless steel more prone to distortion than mild steel?
quiz.explanation: Stainless steel has lower thermal conductivity, so heat concentrates and causes more distortion.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a back purge dam?
options: A) To hold the parts together
B) To contain argon inside the pipe
quiz.explanation: A back purge dam seals the pipe to contain argon and prevent oxidation.

quiz.q: What is the correct torch angle for TIG welding stainless?
quiz.explanation: A 70-80 degree angle allows good visibility and control of the puddle.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of using a CO2/argon mix for TIG welding stainless?
quiz.explanation: CO2 can cause carbon pickup, leading to sensitization and corrosion.

quiz.q: What is the recommended grinding direction for tungsten?
quiz.explanation: Grinding lengthwise creates a stable arc and proper electron flow.

quiz.q: What should you do after welding stainless to restore corrosion resistance?
quiz.explanation: Brushing and pickling removes oxidation and restores the passive layer.
